Commentary.Commentary: Welcome back for England's reply. Out walk the two umpires. The Indian players have taken their respective fielding spots. Danni Wyatt-Hodge and Sophia Dunkley are the two English openers making their way to the crease. And it will be Arundhati Reddy to bowl the first over of the run chase. Dunkley to face. Here we go again.
... THE RUN CHASE ...

A big task ahead to save the series - England may have a very strong head-to-head record against India, but to avoid the repeat of 2025, they will have to execute their second-highest T20I run chase for that. The pitch is slowish, but decent, and the boundaries short, so they have a chance, but scoring quickly has not been their strength this summer. A strong start through their openers is a non-negotiable and India will aim to hit that vulnerable spot right away. An interesting run chase coming up. Stay tuned.

A couple of partnerships helped India recover - England had India wobbling a bit again after Bell's beauty sent Rodrigues back, but Harmanpreet and Deepti Sharma dug in together and stopped the rot. The pair took their time finding their feet, allowing England to keep a lid on things through a quiet middle stretch, but their stand ensured there was no further slide. Once she had her eye in, Kaur found her fluency and began to push on and went on to score a fantastic half-century that saw India touch exactly 180.

England struck early in the first half - Spin did the early damage as India lost both openers inside the first four overs, with Mandhana and Shafali failing to make any impression against the hosts. Yastika Bhatia walked in with positive intent and kept the board ticking, but a run out ended her stay and left India reeling at 60/3, suddenly staring at a serious rebuilding task. That came through a responsible partnership between Rodrigues and skipper Harmanpreet Kaur, as the two added 40 runs together.

Decent finish for the tourists - So India manage to touch that 180-run figure with a good second half overall. There was a bit of a slowdown in the run rate once Rodrigues got out, but they prevented England from making inroads regularly. However, India's running between the wickets was a concern, though, with the batters looking hesitant to push for the quick singles or doubles. England, on the other hand, were equally sharp in the field.

A comical end to the Indian innings. India finish with 180/5. This is fired in full and at the sticks by Sophie. Ghosh digs it out back towards Ecclestone, but with it being the last ball, Kaur sets off for the run. Ghosh had already given up but Sophie fails to gather it cleanly and the ball rolls away to her left. She gets to the ball, turns around and releases an underarm throw at the bowling end with Richa still showing no urgency to complete the run. Ecclestone fails to hit the stumps and the ball dribbles towards long on, allowing the batters to sneak in the second run. Sophie cannot quite believe it and has a sheepish smile on her face. What should have been a dot ball ends up yielding a couple more for India. You never quite know how valuable these runs could prove by the end of the night.

Commentary.Commentary: The wait is over, and we are all set for the decider to get underway. There is a stiff breeze sweeping across the ground, with largely blue skies overhead and only the odd patch of grey cloud in sight. Charlie Dean leads her side out, followed by the two Indian openers, Smriti Mandhana and Shafali Verma. The tall Lauren Bell will open the attack for the home side. Bell to Mandhana. There is a slip in place. Let's go...

England Women (Unchanged Playing XI) - Sophia Dunkley, Danni Wyatt-Hodge, Amy Jones (WK), Alice Capsey, Heather Knight, Freya Kemp, Danielle Gibson, Charlie Dean (C), Sophie Ecclestone, Linsey Smith and Lauren Bell.

India Women (Playing XI) - Smriti Mandhana, Shafali Verma, Yastika Bhatia, Harmanpreet Kaur (C), Jemimah Rodrigues, Richa Ghosh (WK), Deepti Sharma, Arundhati Reddy, Kranti Gaud (In for Shreyanka Patil), Sree Charani and Nandni Sharma.
TOSS - The coin flip lands in favor of the hosts and England Women have elected to BOWL first.

Eyeing to repeat history - The platform for the tourists keeps getting built, and the top order keeps delivering. The problem has been what comes after. Bristol was theirs to take, given their position at 70/1 in the chase, and they still could not find the finish line. So there are some wrinkles to iron out in the middle order. The Indian team will expect more from the dependable duo of Deepti Sharma and Richa Ghosh as it aims to sort out its middle order woes. All in all, the Women in Blue are a team searching for one complete performance, and with the T20 World Cup just a few moons away, Taunton is the perfect place to find it and repeat a series win on English soil, as they did in 2025. Let’s see who trumps this one. Toss and teams up next shortly. Stay tuned.

The hosts aim to dominate - England hold a commanding 25-12 advantage in T20I head-to-head across 37 meetings over India, and on home soil as well, that number tilts largely in their favour, reading 11-8. A captain deputising, a star all-rounder absent, and yet here they are, right in the thick of it. Nat Sciver-Brunt was ruled out of this series due to ongoing rehabilitation from a calf injury, but Charlie Dean’s side rescued a game in Bristol from 116/4, with Freya Kemp’s decisive cameo single-handedly dragging the innings to a total worth defending, and then they went out and defended it. However, the instability in the top order needs to be addressed before heading into the big competition.

Greetings, one and all - From Chelmsford and through Bristol in the south-west of England, and now, this three-match T20I series sets its base in Taunton, the county town of Somerset, which quite literally takes its name from the River Tone that runs through it. Hello and welcome to our coverage of the third and final T20I between England Women and India Women at the Cooper’s Associate County Ground. One win apiece, one game to go, this series has lived up to its billing so far. Let’s hope the decider caps it off perfectly. So hop on for this worthy ride.
... MATCH DAY ...

One last dress rehearsal - The decider has found its home in Taunton. England Women and India Women have been at it all series, splitting the first two T20Is right down the middle and setting up a gripping series finale. India came to Chelmsford and meant business, walking away with the opener. England regrouped, headed to Bristol, and gave a commanding reply to level the series, pushing it into a crucial decider. Now both teams make the trip to Somerset with everything still to play for, and with the ICC Women's T20 World Cup 2026 lurking just around the corner, the stakes could not feel any higher. This is not just a series on the line. This is form, momentum, and confidence heading into the biggest stage of them all. Pride on the line - England carry a point to prove that goes beyond this series. History whispers in their favour at the macro level at home soil, with five series wins against India's two painting a picture of general dominance in this rivalry. But history has a short memory when recent wounds are still raw. The last time Indian women set foot on English soil, they did not just win the series, they owned it. England will be carrying that particular sting into Taunton with plenty of motivation to set the record straight on home soil. India's two series victories in this rivalry came in 2006 and 2025, two very different eras of the game, but both carrying the same message. That they can come here, handle the conditions, handle the pressure, and go home with the trophy. Bowling dominance - England's spinners turned Bristol into a masterclass in suffocation. Charlie Dean, Sophie Ecclestone and Linsey Smith shared 12 overs between them and gave India's batters absolutely nothing to work with, conceding just 77 runs while defending a total that was far from imposing. But the seam has had its say too. Lauren Bell has been the best bowler in this series with five wickets to her name, and since the last T20 World Cup, only Dean has taken more wickets for England than her, with 25 wickets, whereas Dean has picked up 26 to her name. Ecclestone has not been at her sharpest of late, but that has never made her any less dangerous. The world's number one T20I bowler carries that tag for a reason, and on a given day she is the kind of operator who can flip a match on its head almost single-handedly. England will be hoping she saves her best for Taunton, peaking at exactly the right moment with a World Cup waiting just around the corner. Struggles with the bat - England's Powerplay has been a problem they have not solved yet. They have tried two opening pairs already with Capsey in the first and Wyatt-Hodge partnering Dunkley, but they have struggled to click, losing their wickets cheaply in Chelmsford before crawling to 35 for 1 in Bristol without forming a stable platform. Dunkley's form adds another layer of concern. She has not touched or gone beyond 30 since the 2025 series against this same India side, a prolonged dry spell that has quietly become one of England's bigger headaches going into the decider. It has not just been the openers either. Heather Knight and Amy Jones have blown hot and cold across both games, offering glimpses. And looming over all of it is the absence of Nat Sciver-Brunt, whose all-round influence has been missed more evidently. She will not be available for Taunton either. It was Freya Kemp who bailed them out in Bristol with a brilliant cameo, but England cannot rely on singular brilliance. A collective batting effort is not just desirable, it is a requisite. Spin twins and a breakout star - While England's spinners choked India in Bristol, India's own slow-bowling unit has shown it can match them rev for rev. Left-arm spinner Sree Charani weaponised her variations to cause major damage to England's top order, walking away with a brilliant 3/25 in the second game. Complementing her has been the discovery of the tour - the young Nandni Sharma. Her ice-cool 3/34 on debut broke the back of England's chase and proved that India is no longer entirely reliant on established names to bail them out under high pressure. With Deepti Sharma and Shreyanka Patil squeezing the middle overs, India’s bowling group has all the tools required to spin a web around England's fragile batting. Batting blueprints and pacing problems - When India clicks with the bat, they look utterly unstoppable. The opening match in Chelmsford was a masterclass in aggressive recovery, headlined by Jemimah Rodrigues’ fluid 69 and Yastika Bhatia’s anchoring 54. But Bristol exposed a familiar Achilles' heel, pacing through the middle overs against elite spin. The openers, Smriti Mandhana and Shafali Verma, have shown explosive flashes but have lacked the definitive, deep innings conversion required to kill off high-scoring chases. The spotlight in the decider will shine directly on the middle-order engine room. India needs a defining, explosive performance from Richa Ghosh and captain Harmanpreet Kaur, who quietly crossed her 4,000 career T20I runs in Bristol, to ensure India’s scoring rate does not stagnate. Team form (Last 5 completed Women’s T20Is, recent first) ENG-W - WLWLW | IND-W - LWLWL. What to expect? Taunton has historically been a batter’s paradise with short square boundaries, but early on it will offer plenty of assistance to seamers. Once batters get through that tough initial movement, they can score heavily and use the fast outfield to their advantage. Women's T20 cricket returns to The Cooper Associates County Ground of Taunton for the first time since September 2021, and for India, this is only their third visit to this corner of England, the last having come way back in 2011, when the great Jhulan Goswami led the team, and Charlotte Edwards used to lead England at that time. The venue history leans firmly in England's favour, too. Both T20Is played here against India have ended in wins for the hosts, and the broader record tells the same story. England have won 8 of their 11 T20Is at this ground, losing just three, with their last defeat here dating all the way back to 2018. England have a chance to win back-to-back T20I series on home soil, having already beaten New Zealand last month, and a win here would send them into the World Cup on a real crest. India's motivation is no less sharp. The big event is less than two weeks away, and how you arrive at a tournament matters. Turning up on the back of a series defeat is not the story they want to be telling.
